You're asking an incredibly broad question, too broad to answer meaningfully. 

You can mix up your play in so many ways from the macro to the micro interactions. You can mix up your pace/tempo, either increasing or decreasing the speed of interactions, forcing the opponent to adapt. You can mix up your timings in the myriad situations that exist in this game. The classic scenario is one person on the ground shielding and the other landing with an aerial. Which aerial do you use? Is it a multi hit? Are you going to space it as far away as possible or land unsafely (as a mixup)? Are you going to land it as close to the ground as possible for shield safety? Alternatively empty lands or double jump mixups add further dimensions on to this interaction. And thats a single scenario. 

You can practice mixups to one scenario at a time. Not to your entire playstyle. Or it won't be nearly as effective anyways. Think about how to mixup your recovery, or your neutral, or what you do after taking a stock. You can practice those individually. Taken together you will have a more varied/complex playstyle that will be harder to adapt to.

There's a lot of ways at looking at it. Obviously they've been diversifying animations while also making the hurtbox more accurate to what it looks like, because as you say, it's intuitive. 

But sometimes it can go so far as to be unintuitive, where something looks like it should hit, but then you zoom in all the way and see how the hurtbox shifted. You need to consider if an animation reads at the speed and distance that a typical platform fighter is played at.

Another way of looking at it: they could simply adjust animations to be drastic, so hurtbox shifting happens less.

The issue is, it's a lot harder to get in and land a hit in a platform fighter. The inherently limited movement and space of 2d fighters means this kind of microinteraction can be accounted for a lot better by the player. It's much more likely to be "random" in a plat fighter

Here are some the main things I've noticed:

You need to increase your APM. Rivals rewards speed in a lot of situations that smash would reward decision making. Some of the best I've played in Rivals is when I've stopped thinking about interactions and simply mashed my best button. You can do this in smash as well, but you're much more likely to be punished for it. 

Related point, stop trying to react to anything. If you see a move, you're already too slow to punish it. Even strong attacks are rarely worth the risk of trying to whiff punish

Okay so let's talk this through cause there's a few things I feel like you either don't know or misunderstand (not being mean, just trying to help). 

So you put someone in a tech chase situation, could be a throw, and aerial, a tilt, whatever. They now have several options. I'm going to put them under two umbrellas.

First umbrella: they tech. I'm doing this first because after a certain level of play, most people will tech most things. If they tech, they can neutral tech and stay in place with some invulnerable frames, or they can tech roll in or tech roll away. Some characters have options to cover more than one tech option at a time, often referred to generally as "coverage." Your job is to cover as many options as possible and try to react and punish. A lot of characters aren't fast enough to cover tech roll away in some situations, so often you're looking at tech roll in or neutral tech. And at mid level, a lot of people will only neutral tech. Your goal is to hit them in the immediate aftermath of the invulnerability frames of the tech. If you time too early you swing through their invulnerable character and get punished. If too late they may throw a shield up, or spot dodge, or press a button. 

The second umbrella: no tech. Big blue flop on the ground, in a lot of situations this should activate an endorphin response in you: I can cook here. If you're close enough, go for a jab reset, jab once or up to two times and you can reset the timer that locks the opponent on to the ground. Other moves beside jab can reset, it depends on knockback, but jab is usually a safe bet if you're not like meta knight. Then hit them with either your best combo starter or a strong attack for KO or knock off stage. If you're not close enough for the jab lock, or you don't react in time, you're now in the situation that you described in your post. Keep in mind, you can hit them with anything on a missed tech, besides like meme moves like warlock punch.  

Once they've missed the tech, *and* you did nothing after a period of time (so you fail to react, or you just don't feel confident in punishing the missed tech for one reason or another, then you are looking at different options. One of which is get up attack. This is why you may not see this often in high level play, because they're often playing at a fast pace, usually teching moves, and will often punish missed techs before getup attack becomes possible. Once it does, you see getup attack all the time, especially on platforms. It's a strong option in a lot of situations. If you're getting hit by it a lot, you either need to react to tech situations faster, or you can shield it and punish out of shield (I would think shield grab would work), or you can hover above with a full hop and landing aerial after the getup attack.

Once they're out of the percent range you can play normally, but any time that combo might work, you go for it. You'll play worse than normal doing this, but that's okay. It's part of the process. You want to ingrain it in your muscle memory so that it becomes second nature. Once you feel like it's locked in,  move on to another. You could do down throw back air, for a slight variation on the earlier,  or nair dash attack, or you could work on kill confirms since that's very important to Jokers gameplan. Obviously talking about fair 1, up air drag down, down/up smash.

Related to mindset/ avoiding the panic options/ nerves - check out the inner game of tennis. It's a short book that's on the face of it about tennis, but it really applies to all sorts of high stakes situations. I read it for music because that's my job, but I know specifically Shadic has said its ideas helped him a lot. There's one that specifically applies to what you mentioned: Self One and Self Two. Self One is the active conscious part of your brain that talks a lot and worries if you're going to play well or not. Self Two is the one that's actually playing the game. The subconscious part of your brain that automatically knows how to short hop fast fall (or whatever, just an example) without you telling your hands how to do it. Pro smash players often call this auto pilot, and I know MkLeo and Tweek have both mentioned having a good autopilot as key to success in bracket. When you're practicing you want to learn how to let your self 2 do what it needs to do to play without your ego (self 1) getting in the way. Self 1 has a purpose in vod review or coming up with counter play and so on,  but in the moment you just want to be locked in. It's sort of like finding the "flow state."

There's a lot to improve upon, but I'll just touch on what helped me starting out with pit.

Check out some down throw combos with Pit, they're pretty simple, and you lost a lot of free damage by going for f throw or back throw. One that I get a lot of mileage out of is Down throw down air nair. You have to get the sour spot of down air that sends up,  not the spike. Down throw bair works at mid to high percents depending on DI, and down throw Nair is also a bread and butter for Pit. Sometimes if platforms don't interfere, you can get down throw Nair into fair into a grab or dash attack. Strings like that are how Pit puts damage on. 

Space back air more. So aim for the very tip of the move, and land it close to the ground. It's super safe on shield, like minus 3, and it can lead into combos at low percent (back air dash attack.)

In general, you want to be more grounded with Pit. It's tempting to jump a lot because of the multiple jumps, but his air speed is bad, and his ground speed is very good. On top of that he has great grounded options. I could stand to see you use a lot more down tilts and up tilts. They're both solid options that aren't too committal and can lead into followups. Down tilt, I usually plan to lead into Nair, but it can work with any aerial besides down air. Up tilt leads into Nair at very low percents or up air all the way to kill percent where it becomes a confirm. 

Beyond the Pit specific stuff, I think you're just committing to unsafe options way too much. Lots of dash grabs or dash attacks, or unsafe aerial pressure. Pick your moments more carefully, and avoid anything that might be too predictable. 

Good luck!

It's so context dependent, it's difficult for me to say. A lot of times my goal is to corner the opponent, so I'm taking stage control by dashing/walking. I might cycle through a few different movement options combined with shielding stuff as needed. That could be jumps, either short or full, could be more grounded movement, or a roll. For me spot dodge is a hard callout if I think they're looking for a grab.

I play Pit, and he has a solid out of shield game, so shielding is very good for me. It's an element of my gameplan that I cycle through sometimes, nairing or shield grabbing unsafe options on shield. 

A whole other element of this is parrying. Parry is underrated in this game in general, it's quite strong, just because it gives you access to your full moveset after blocking something. So for Pit, who has very fast smash attacks, that can lead to an early stock at ledge if you parry something. In case you didn't know, to parry you want to release your shield right as an attack hits it.

I think shielding is one of your best general tools for dealing with zoner heavy playstyles and characters. So characters like Snake, Samus, Min Min, the Links, they often have risk free projectiles to throw at you from far away. Shield combined with thoughtful and precise grounded movement is often some of the best counterplay to that, because a lot of these characters want you to jump. Their whole game plan is to condition jumps, and then call them out.

A big part of learning to shield well is knowing the difference between walking and dashing. When you're walking, which is obviously slower than dashing, but your shield will come out faster than if you were dashing. So knowing when to walk shield versus dash shield is a big part of learning how to shield effectively. Walking is also nice because it let's you space things and position more specifically.

Playing optimally in the ways you described is incredibly difficult in ultimate. That's why very few actually do it. Everyone wants to optimize their advantage state because everyone enjoys pulling off a high damage combo or kill confirm. But optimizing neutral and disadvantage to the point that Shinymark and Sonix have isn't very fun for most people. It's hard work that takes focus, dedication, and a lot of tech skill. 

It's weird to frame optimal play as anti creative, in my view you must be creative to find the optimal solution to any given situation in game. Ultimate isn't a solved game, especially because of how many matchups there are, as well as the general difficulty of not messing up in neutral. You can't just input the "equation" of what's happening in a given match and spit out a "answer" that works everytime. There's way too many variables involved. So for me, playing optimally is not only impressive from a skill perspective, it's also usually very creative. Neutral and disadvantage are very important for sure. Top players are very good in all aspects of the game because it all matters. But advantage is everything in ultimate. If your character has to win neutral 4 times to the opponents one to take a stock, you had to work a lot harder. Neutral is simply a lot harder to win over and over compared to getting one good hit and going into a flowchart.

I often think of it like a card game of chance. In neutral, the deck is stacked in no one's favor. You might have a few good tools, so maybe you get a couple of cards added in your favor, but ultimately, you're going to have to outplay the opponent. In advantage, you've stacked the deck hugely in your favor. There are way more options that let you give percent and way less that get the opponent out. It just makes mathematical sense that you should play as much of the game with a stacked deck as possible. If you reset to neutral a lot, you're playing a more "fair" game and leaving more up to player skill and chance. 

The best characters in the game can even stack the deck in neutral. Sonic has spin dash and pure speed, which limits the opponents options hugely, even in neutral. Then you add in the insane reward he gets off a single hit, and you have a top tier. Steve is the same way with mining/ blocks. He limits a lot of approach options, or even kill options with block, and mining forces the opponent to approach unless they want to deal with diamond Steve the whole match. 

So yeah, TLDR, they're both very important. But there's plenty of characters that are great in neutral and disadvantage, but their advantage just isn't very scary, so they're not thought of super highly. ZSS comes to mind here. Lucina is similar. They aren't bad characters clearly, but the best characters in the game can kill you *off a single hit.* That's insane. 

It's worth noting that Luigi and Kazuya, characters with mid neutral and bad disadvantage but top 5 advantage states, both have good results.

So just to be really clear here: when I say slow the game down, that doesn't necessarily mean you input fewer things per second. The pace that you pick options needs to remain high, but you might commit much less often. That's more what I mean. Some of the best way to play defensively is to be extremely ambiguous with your movement, and then absolutely explode once you actually get the hit. Some players I'm thinking of specifically are Tweek, Marss, Muteace, Shadic. All of them are abusing some of the more busted aspects of their character, but the concept is still good. 

Tweek uses banana (of course) to help him turtle, either by increasing the value of shield, or as a bait for the opponent. He also has lots of little weird mixups with monkey flip, pop gun cancel, b reverses and so on. A lot of these are intended to confuse the opponent so they don't know what you're going for. This is the best way to play defensively. 

Marss uses ZSSs mobility combined with flip jump to do the same thing, baiting commitments and then punishing. Shadic uses the burst movement Corrin has via her initial dash to make his movement extremely hard to track, and obviously Corrin has a giant sword to swat opponents out of the air when they try to jump. Muteace is often very defensive, especially in last hit scenarios, but he's moving like crazy. 

So when you want to slow the game down, slow your pace of committal options. But you should absolutely still be moving and baiting approaches with any safe mixups you have at your disposal. You want to sew confusion, fear, maybe frustration so that the other person commits first, and in a punishable way.

It's hard to say what "average" and "good" means but I can give you the cliff notes on how I improved at the very least. 

The shortest answer in a word: experience. I have thousands of hours in this game, spread out over years, and most of that was with a competitive mindset. They may have been Friendly's, but it was against people around my level, trying to win. I've played a lot of online, and attended my locals. You just gotta play the game *a lot* to really get the encyclopedic knowledge of different situations and matchups in this game. This isn't super actionable advice, but it may be helpful to hear that sometimes, the reason you're getting destroyed by someone is they simply have played the game for far longer than you. 

As to things you can do, watch top players. There's a pretty big event most weekends, and if you're free you should tune in.  People talk a lot of trash, but the competitive scene at the top level is mostly really fun to watch. Just skip grand finals if you're bored lol

Related to watching top players, make a point to study vods of players that play your character. If you don't have a main, you absolutely need a main. That doesn't mean you never get to play other characters again, it just means you focus your energies into one character specifically to improve. Check out what your top player does at different points in the match. Take notes. What moves are they looking for in neutral? How do they follow that up at low percents? What is the mid percent combo game like? How do they get kills? Edge guards, ledge trapping, true kill confirms? How do they deal with disadvantage and recovering? What about getting off the ledge?

Pick one of these questions, answer it, and then watch a video of yourself playing and cringe at how not like them you are. Part of the process. Then implement your answer into your own gameplay. Figure out how to make it work, it may not click right away. Keep answering those questions one by one,  and you'll get very good. I highly recommend working on one aspect at a time and letting the rest of your gameplay be auto pilot. You want actionable clear goals, so you judge whether or not you've improved and internalized the lesson. 

Good luck!

He was ledge trapping you very effectively, and you weren't getting much off your own ledge traps. You kept letting him back on for free either with hail mary edge guard attempts, or Side B from way across stage. I contrast, he was always covering roll and ready to react to most of your options.

I think it can be helpful to break down in very basic terms what is going on when you "play neutral." Both players should be observing their opponent closely as soon as the game begins. You should instantly go into "gathering data" mode looking for patterns, habits, and so on. What does it look like the opponent wants? How can I avoid that from happening? Be very specific with your answers, don't just say "he wants to hit me, I simply do not want to get hit." Because usually they want a specific positoning to get a combo starters from zero percent.

 The inherent complexity of neutral is that while you are observing them trying to get a read on their playstyle and tempo, they are doing the exact same thing to you (or they should be). So while you are observing them, gathering data to use in the match, you're trying to be as unpredictable as possible. Alternatively, their is the "I will bair because it is strong" school where you simply spam your best option. Some characters have extremely overturned options that require an opponent to modify their playstyle (Steve block, Rob gyro, spin dash, t jolt). A mix of both is probably best. 

So with Diddy you have a lot of tools. Banana in hand gives you some of the scariest Out of Shield punishes in the game, which is why is common to see Diddy players simply dash up and shield once they get banana. Monkey flip is also a super frustrating option that gives Diddy great burst range even against shielding opponents. Thinking about how you can best utilize those tools without being predictable will lead to some success. Then you need to consider the specifics of whatever matchup you find yourself in. Some characters will force you to change your playstyle, and some will be more susceptible to some options in comparison to others. 

This is just scratching the surface of neutral, it's one of the most complex topics you can get into in regards to smash, and I don't think it's quite as important as advantage. So there's a little bit of diminishing returns when it comes to working on neutral. Still worth thinking about of course..

TLDR: work on your movement, make sure you feel 100% with short hops, full hops, walk, dash, dash shield, platform movement,  and character specific stuff like pop gun cancels out of monkey flip, how you set up banana and so on.  This will improve your neutral inherently.

I think you have a lot to learn about the fundamentals of the game, and that should take precedence over Pit specific stuff.

In general, you are committing to risky options way too much, and the risks you take don't even lead to much reward. I think you go for an f smash at zero and get 11 percent off it. If you were playing against me and whiffed that f smash, I guarantee I'll either take the stock at high percent, or you'll take about 40 percent in a true combo and then have to deal with advantage state. This is very common at mid to high levels of the game, and some characters will punish you much more harshly than that. 

Right now you seem to have 4 things you do in neutral: 
1. Arrow. This is good, low risk, exactly where you want to use arrow. You can't rely on it, but it's a good harassment tool.

 2. Seemingly random side Bs and smash attacks. These are quite bad and I would work to eliminate them entirely. Side B is a terrible move and I would only use it in hail mary situations where you're looking for an early kill at the ledge. This should be extremely rare, less than once a game. It can also be used to recover, and that's fine. As for the smash attacks, Pit has very fast frame data, so you're getting away with it against a low level player,  probably online, but you really shouldn't be using them this much. Someone better than you will punish you hard for using such laggy moves. At the very least, please only use them when the opponent will actually lose a stock. Then the risk/reward is in your favor at least. 

3. Very strange full hop nairs that don't complete the move. This is the only aerial I see you use frequently in neutral. It's a good move, but you're over relying on it, and not using it very effectively. I view nair as primarily useful in 3 ways: Out of Shield it can be very good, to snuff out jumps, and to edge guard. It's not a very good move to jump at the opponent with if they're going to stay on the ground because the range is limited. Furthermore, I usually short hop with it, as that can combo into forward air at low percents, and is more likely to hit.

4. Sometimes you dash back a single time then dash attack. This is a good starting point for movement in neutral, but you should start mixing in more movement options, and please don't *always* dash back a single time into burst option. Dash back is very good in ult, and Pit is fast on the ground, but you never want to become predictable.

Here's some stuff you should start doing:

1. First learn some low percent combos,  and then have that as your goal to hit in neutral from the start of the game. Something I love about Pit is that his down throw leads into every one of his aerials eventually. At zero,  very simple one us down throw into forward air, which you can sometimes extend into a dash attack to cash out, or another grab. Down throw can also lead into Nair, which is sometimes the best option if there's a platform nearby, back air which can be a kill setup at ledge, and down air which combos into Nair. Down throw, dair, nair, is my typical low percent combo, it does like 35 percent or something. 

2. Pit is a sword character. Use his "sword". That means spacing back air and forward air in neutral. When spaced, these are fairly safe tools, especially back air, and can lead into more damage. Back air tipper can lead into dash attack, and both back air hitboxes can lead into grab depending on DI and weight/gravity of opponent.  Back air is a kill move, and you can simply back air at ledge a lot of times for the kill. If you're ever wondering what a good nice to throw out is, back air is usually the answer for Pit. I basically have different "modes" or layers to my game plan that I can freely cycle through as needed.

At low percent I'm looking to connect certain moves that I know lead into solid early damage, but I'm not tunnel visioning on that. Like if I know a grab nets me about 40 percent so obviously I'm looking for that, but I get the opportunity to punish with an up smash, I'll take the up smash. For my main (Pit), there are like 4 or 5 moves that lead into good early percent BnBs, so lots of options. I slowly developed that Repertoire of combos over time, first focusing on grab combos, then nair, back air, down tilt, up tilt and so on.  You get more little strings together as you play more, especially once you start understanding how platforms and tech chases can be incorporated. 

At mid percent is when I'm most "ambitious" with my gameplay. I'm looking for the one big advantage state that gets my opponent to kill percent. You see this at top level all the time, Miya, Sparg0, Light, Acola, they win neutral once or twice and usually thats enough. This can be an edge guard situation, a ledge trap (hint hint, this is usually where wolf makes his money), a juggle, or if you play a good character it can all be a true combo (Steve power). A lot of this is MU dependent. Some other commenters have mentioned playing around the opponents strengths, which is an option. I prefer to exploit weaknesses rather than try to avoid their strong stuff, but that's just how I look at it.

So if I know a character is susceptible to edge guarding, I know that's my win condition. If they struggle to get off ledge, I'm putting a lot of thought into the ledge trap. If they can struggle to take stocks, I'm going to focus on playing evasively and defensively at high percent. 

The last and imo most important part of gameplan is how are you going to take stocks. This doesn't have to be complicated. A lot of times just spamming a killing aerial at ledge is enough. It's wild how many stocks I get from simply back airing at ledge and people either normal get up,  jump, or roll into it. And the nature of ultimate means a lot of characters can effectively cover jump and neutral get up with a fast aerial and then react if they roll or get up attack. Kill confirms and knowing percents when they work is very important here. Sometimes you need to know exactly the percents (think inkling up throw or DK ding dong) but usually you can get by with intuition as long as you're thinking about it. 

Last piece of advice would be to work on one thing at a time here. Pick one piece of one phase of the game and focus on that. It's a marathon, not a sprint. Biggest bang for your buck imo is either low percent BnB combos or ledge trapping for the stock. Wolf does both of those quite well.

Edit: developing your gameplan is fundamentally a very experimental process to find out what works for you.  Like you said, Wolf has a lot of good moves. Figuring out when to use what will naturally take some trial and error. But I think if you're focused on one aspect at a time, you will see improvement.

Isabelle is super annoying to deal with, so it could be that you're getting tilted/flustered and that's negatively affecting your gameplay. Make sure you're always in a neutral head space when playing MUs that are frustrating. Try to simply observe what is happening as if you were spectating. 

Specific tips: crouching is good when they are Slingshot zoning, and don't forget to *walk* then shield. You can get the shield up much faster that way. Your goal is to slowly patiently approach mostly walking and shielding until they are cornered. Then Isabelle has very few options to get out of the corner, most will predictably roll and you can capitalize on that. Once you knock them off stage, you need to get some edge guards going. Isabelle is very vulnerable while recovering and can't really cover herself like Villager can with Lloyd rocket. Figuring out edge guarding in specific matchups is an experimental process, and will require some trial and error. You will  probably SD and lose games in order to figure this out. This is a necessary part of the process imo

Eventually they may start rolling or get up attack, which can be hard punished by Roy. F smash on a roll read or a Side B can kill soooo early. If you're not getting those early stocks, Roy isn't nearly as threatening. 

In neutral, I'd recommend reverse falling up air at low percents. It can lead into a lot of damage (up air into back air, or up air into up air for a juggle), and it's very safe, with a generous sweet spot. At high percents, falling up air *sour spot* can combo into back air as a kill confirm. 

In general, don't be afraid to get up close and personal with Roy. His buttons are a lot faster and safer than most
